analysis: The PR contains only documentation and a changelog: a new `darkbloom sandbox` command group, a docs index link and a CLI reference section. No Swift source is supplied, so the implementation (SandboxInstaller, SandboxAddon, SandboxCommand) is unreviewed. The security-relevant behavior described is: (1) setup downloads install.sh over HTTPS (redirects only to https, 1 MiB cap, `#!` shell check, 0600 file in a 0700 directory) and runs it with /bin/sh without CLI-side signature verification, and `--server` is user-overridable; (2) the CLI drives the closed-source add-on `darkbloom-sandbox` (status/pause/resume/uninstall) with bounded timeouts, and reads `agent/agent.log`; (3) `darkbloom status` adds a Sandboxes line limited to 2 s so the add-on cannot hang the CLI; (4) it refuses sudo; (5) the installer's JSON progress is parsed leniently, and the installer's output is rendered to the terminal, which could carry terminal escape sequences from an untrusted installer. The sandbox add-on shares the Mac with inference, and the doc says inference pauses during jobs. This touches TB-012 and A-018 (add-on hold), but coordinator and add-on behavior are outside the evidence. The threat model has no boundary for the installer and add-on supply chain, which I reported as new attack surface. Open questions for deeper review: the real Swift implementation, whether the installer authenticates its release, whether the add-on's privileges and hold handling match TB-012 and T-059/T-060, and whether the `--server` override is restricted in code.

findings.detail: The new `darkbloom sandbox setup` flow, as documented, downloads `<server>/install.sh` and runs it with `/bin/sh` as the logged-in user. The CLI checks only TLS, HTTP 200, a 1 MiB cap and a `#!` line, and the doc states it does not verify the script beyond TLS. The `--server` option accepts any https URL without credentials. This is a download-and-execute path in the same user account that holds `~/.darkbloom` (provider token, local token, add-on socket) and the provider's other local state. If the sandbox service, its CDN, a TLS-trusted intermediary, or a social-engineered `--server` value serves a malicious script, it gets user-level code execution on provider Macs. Release verification happens inside the script it would replace, so it cannot protect against a hostile script. The threat model has no boundary or threat for this installer path or the closed-source add-on. Fix: pin the script by a signature or hash checked in the CLI, or embed a signed release manifest. Restrict `--server` to an allowlist or a dev-only flag. Add a boundary entry and threat for the installer and add-on supply chain.
findings.title: Sandbox setup runs a TLS-only, unsigned install.sh as the provider user, with no matching threat-model coverage
